::: {.why}
Order selection is model selection under a different name, and the criteria disagree for a reason you can state precisely, which matters more here than in most fields because the true model is not in the set.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- State what AIC and BIC each estimate, and why BIC selects a smaller model as the sample grows.
- Say which criterion you would use for a forecasting model and which for an inference claim, and defend the split.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>60 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [20 min]{.task-min} Write out the two penalties and their motivations from memory, then check them: AIC targets predictive risk and BIC approximates a marginal likelihood under a prior on models. Say what each one assumes about whether the true model is in the candidate set.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [30 min]{.task-min} Run the simulation that settles it: generate 500 series from a known AR(2), and record how often AIC and BIC each recover the true order at sample sizes of 250, 1,000 and 5,000. Report a table of recovery rates. Then repeat with data generated from a process that is not in your candidate set at all and see what each criterion does.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [10 min]{.task-min} Try StatsForecast's AutoARIMA on the same series and compare its choice against your grid. It is the tool most people reach for and it is worth knowing what it optimises before you use its output.
:::
:::
